problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-5 & -2 & -3 \\ -1 & -6 & -3 \\ 5 & 10 & 11\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 8\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}-4 & a & -1 \\ 2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & b & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=PD{P}^{-1},$ find the value of $\frac{a}{b}.$

activity_context.topic_title: Diagonalizing a 3x3 Matrix in the General Case

examples.knowledge_point: Diagonalizing a 3x3 Matrix Given Part of the Diagonalization
examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070007/assets/055da79921f7640b8f396653160a3ec34c4959ee4157806c0286152fa781c3aa.png)
Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=PDP^{-1},$ find the value of $\dfrac{a}{b}.$
examples.worked_solution:
Notice that $D=P^{-1}AP$ is a diagonalization of the matrix $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we find that the eigenvalues of $A$ are

$\qquad$ $\lambda_1=\lambda_3=-2 \quad$ and $\quad \lambda_2=-9.$

The second column of $P$ corresponds to $\lambda=-2.$ Computing $A-\lambda I,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & -2 \\ -2 & -4 & 4 \\ 3 & 3 & -8\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -2 \\ -2 & -2 & 4 \\ 3 & 3 & -6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -2 & 0 \\ -2 & -2 & 4 & 0 \\ 3 & 3 & -6 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, $x_2$ and $x_3$ are free variables. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
x_1 = -x_2+2x_3.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070007/assets/c6dbdd2b14d7b81925ed2d7a10441061a5aaed814d9a295dd097597431985f0b.png)

Comparing this with the second column of $P,$ we deduce that $x_2=0.$ Now, setting $x_3=1$ and substituting our values for $x_2$ and $x_3$ into the general solution, we obtain the following: 

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, $\dfrac{a}{b}=\dfrac{2}{1}=2.$

feedback.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 & -3 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -3\end{aligned}]
$$

If the matrix $A$ above is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix $D.$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 6 & -3 \\ 0 & -2-\lambda  & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-2-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & -3 \\ 1 & -3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-2-\lambda )((1-\lambda )(-3-\lambda )+3) & =0 \\ -(\lambda +2)({\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda ) & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda +2)^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=0$ (simple root) and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2$ (double root).

Let's now find the dimension of the eigenspace corresponding to each eigenvalue.

- First, we consider the simple root ${\lambda }_{1}=0.$ Since the root is simple, the dimension of the eigenspace ${V}_{0}$ corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=0$ is

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{0})=1.
$$

- Next, we consider the double root ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ Let's find the dimension of the eigenspace ${V}_{-2}$ corresponding to this eigenvalue. To do this, we row-reduce the matrix $A-(-2)I:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 & -3 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -3\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 6 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-\frac{1}{3}){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & 6 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & 6 & -3 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). This implies that we will have $3-2=1$ linearly independent eigenvector corresponding to the current eigenvalue. So, 

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{-2})=1.
$$

Therefore, $A$ is *not* diagonalizable, since 

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{0})+\text{dim}({V}_{-2})=1+1=2\ne 3.\,\times 
$$
